title: SOXQ ETF Is A Sharper Bet Than Its Name Suggests
detail:
SOXQ ETF Is A Sharper Bet Than Its Name Suggests
Trefis Team

IWM
QQQ
IVZ
SPY
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

A fund's label tells you the category, but a look at the holdings ledger reveals the actual shape of your investment.

While the Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF (SOXQ) holds 32 different stocks, the fund's portfolio behaves like about 18 equally weighted holdings. That small gap between the number on the box and the reality of the portfolio is where the real story of any index fund lives. The fund aims to track the performance of the largest U.S.-listed companies in the semiconductor business, giving investors exposure to the building blocks of modern electronics.

But an exchange-traded fund is more than just a list of names. It is a basket where some holdings carry far more weight than others. Understanding that weighting is key to knowing what you truly own.

How Many Bets Are You Really Making?

The fund's concentration becomes clear when you look at the top of the portfolio. The ten largest holdings make up 62% of the fund's total assets. This means the performance of a handful of companies has an outsized impact on the fund's daily moves. The single largest holding is Nvidia (NVDA) at 12.4% of the fund, followed by other industry heavyweights like Broadcom (AVGO) and Micron Technology (MU).

When just a few names command this much of the portfolio, their fortunes disproportionately shape your returns. This kind of focused exposure is common in thematic funds, and a look inside another popular semiconductor ETF reveals a similar structure.

Where Is The Money Actually Going?

The fund's name promises semiconductor exposure, and it delivers. But even within that category, the capital is tilted toward specific corners of the industry. The fund is almost entirely in the Information Technology sector, but the breakdown inside is what matters. The Semiconductors sub-industry accounts for 75% of the fund. The next-largest slice is Semiconductor Materials & Equipment, which makes up 23% of the portfolio.

Together, these two slivers of the market define nearly the entire fund. The result is an investment heavily weighted toward chip designers and the companies that supply them with manufacturing machinery.

Is This The Shape You Intended?

Knowing a fund's internal composition is not about judging it as good or bad. It is about alignment. The Invesco PHLX Semiconductor ETF offers a distinct, concentrated position on the semiconductor industry. The key question for an investor is whether this specific shape, with its heavy reliance on a few top names and sub-industries, is the exposure you were looking for, or if it doubles up on bets you have already made elsewhere in your portfolio.

title: Time To Take Profits In XLV?
detail:
Time To Take Profits In XLV?
Trefis Team

Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

The healthcare fund just printed a record high, but cashing out of a steady compounder is often the wrong move.

A new high always feels like a moment of decision. For holders of the State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLV), that moment is now. The fund just closed at $167.26, its highest level ever, after a +16.6% run over the past three months. When you see a gain like that, the natural question is whether to hold on, trim your stake, or get out entirely. XLV is an exchange-traded fund designed to give you a slice of the healthcare industry within the S&P 500, holding everything from pharmaceuticals to medical equipment companies.

How Solid Is This New Peak?

Before you act, it is worth looking at what drove this high. First, this is a concentrated fund. Its holdings sit "almost entirely in one sector, Health Care," making it a single-industry allocation. The recent advance was also driven by a few key names. While participation was wide, with 24 of the 30 largest holdings rising over the past three months, the actual heavy lifting was done by a few. The "three biggest movers accounted for about 56% of the up-and-down price movement" among those top 30 holdings. On top of that, the basket is not cheap by its own historical standards. The fund's holdings now trade at about 31.0 times earnings, compared to a roughly 5-year median of 26.8 for this fund.

So, What Should A Holder Do Now?

With the fund looking stretched and trading at a richer valuation, the temptation to sell is real. But for a long-term investor, the most sensible action is often the hardest one: do nothing. A new high, by itself, is not a signal to sell a quality asset. It is what you want your investments to do. This is compounding at work. Selling a fund that holds 63 positions across a vital sector just because it's performing well can be a classic mistake, forcing you to pay taxes and find a new home for your capital. The price of earning long-term returns includes weathering volatility. The fund's deepest fall in recent years was 17.1%, a figure that provides context for what a significant pullback could look like.

The fund currently sits about 10.3% above its 200-day moving average, which confirms it has run ahead of its trend. The only strong reason to act may have nothing to do with the market and everything to do with your own plan. If this strong performance has made your XLV position significantly larger than its target weight in your portfolio, trimming it back into line is simply disciplined rebalancing. This question of what to do at a new high is not unique to healthcare; other sectors like financials are facing similar moments.

CSD's 29-stock spin-off strategy returned 53% over the past year, nearly doubling VEGN's 30% gain with far less tech concentration.

Both funds crushed SPY's 16% annual return, but VEGN's semiconductor tilt makes it largely redundant for investors already holding QQQ.

VEGN behaves like a duration trade dressed as an ethics screen, making it vulnerable whenever rising rates reprice mega-cap semis.

Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and US Vegan Climate didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today.

Two rules-based ETFs, both beating the S&P 500, have almost nothing else in common. Invesco S&P Spin-Off ETF (NYSEARCA:CSD) versus US Vegan Climate ETF (NASDAQ:VEGN): one is a concentrated basket of corporate castoffs; the other is a tech-heavy large-cap fund filtered through animal-welfare and climate screens. Both have outrun the index, but their underlying engines differ fundamentally, and that difference dictates when each fund wins.

24/7 Wall St.
What Each Fund Is Actually Betting On

CSD holds recently separated U.S. companies, typically within roughly four years of a spin-off, tracking the S&P U.S. Spin-Off Index. It is a catalyst strategy betting that newly independent management teams, cleaner capital structures, and forced institutional selling around separation create a mispricing window. The portfolio is tiny by ETF standards, holding about 30 positions with heavy weights in industrial and infrastructure spin-offs like GE Vernova at 9.3%, Qnity at 8.0%, and GE HealthCare at 6.9%. SanDisk, at 9.5%, is the largest single equity. This is a mid-cap, cyclical, industrial-tilted basket with essentially zero overlap with the S&P 500's mega-cap leadership.

Act now: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just named his top 10 AI stocks — and US Vegan Climate didn't make the cut. Grab the names FREE today.

VEGN runs the opposite trade. Its Beyond Investing US Vegan Climate Index starts with the U.S. large-cap universe and excludes companies tied to animal exploitation, fossil fuel extraction, defense, tobacco, and human rights abuses. What survives resembles the Nasdaq-100 with financials added. Top holdings are Micron at 5.9%, AMD at 4.6%, Applied Materials at 3.9%, and Apple at 3.8%. Semiconductors and software dominate. The implicit bet is that ethical screens push toward asset-light, high-margin businesses that win in growth regimes.

Where the Difference Shows Up

The past year makes the contrast clear. CSD returned 53.0% over the trailing 12 months and is up 34.5% year to date. VEGN returned 30.0% over one year and 20.6% year to date. SPY is up 16.3% over one year and 8.6% YTD. QQQ trailed VEGN slightly at 18.9% over the year.

title: How Much Of Your Portfolio Is Really Apple (AAPL)?
detail:
How Much Of Your Portfolio Is Really Apple (AAPL)?
Trefis Team
Tue, July 28, 2026 at 11:40 AM EDT 4 min read
SPY
IWM
DIA
QQQ
AAPL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by ColiN00B on Pixabay

You bought a diversified fund, but one high-flying stock may now be quietly driving your returns and your risk.

Apple (AAPL) stock is held across 66 of the equity funds in our universe, and in some cases, the position is anything but small. If you own a broad technology or large-cap growth fund, you likely have a bigger, more concentrated position in this one consumer electronics and software company than you ever decided on. After a powerful run-up, it is worth taking a moment to see the single-stock risk you may have inherited.

How Stretched Has The Stock Become?

By one simple measure, the stock is extended. Apple now trades about 22% above its 200-day moving average, a technical cushion built on a +58% return over the past year. That momentum has been particularly strong recently, with a +24% return in just the last three months. This is not a prediction, but a scenario: if the stock simply fell back to its 200-day average, it would mean a drop of about 18% from its current price. The stock also trades at about 38 times its expected earnings for the year ahead.

Which Of Your Funds Are Riding It Hardest?

The funds with the heaviest exposure to Apple have been rewarded handsomely. The concentration that powered their gains is the same concentration that now represents single-name risk. The most exposed recognizable fund is Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF (FTEC), which holds about 17.1% of its assets in Apple and returned +32% over the past year. Others are close behind. Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) has about 14.3% in the stock and returned +31%, while State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK) holds about 13.3% and delivered a +34% return.

What A Pullback Would Actually Cost You

Let's translate that concentration into concrete numbers using our reversion scenario. If Apple were to fall 18%, the direct hit to these funds from this one stock would be significant. The Fidelity MSCI Information Technology Index ETF (FTEC) would lose about 3.1% of its value from its Apple holding alone. For Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT), the loss would be about 2.6%, and for iShares U.S. Technology ETF (IYW), it would be about 2.5%.

Making this exposure sticky is the tax trap. You cannot surgically sell just the Apple shares inside your ETF. To reduce your position, you must sell the entire fund, which could trigger a taxable capital gain, making it difficult to trim a position that has quietly grown.

The fund's new peak feels like a moment to act, but the right move for this broad value portfolio might be the simplest one.

A new high can feel like a finish line, but the Vanguard Value ETF (VTV) has given back 17.0% from a peak before. This is an index fund built to track large, value-oriented U.S. companies. After closing at a record $221.72, a gain of +9.5% in just three months, it is natural to wonder if you should lock in that profit.

How Solid Is This Foundation?

At its core, the fund is well-diversified. Its holdings span 8 sectors, with Financials the largest at about 27% of the main positions. And on the surface, the recent advance looks broad. Over the past three months, 25 of the 30 largest holdings rose. But a closer look shows the force of the move was concentrated. The three biggest movers accounted for about 55% of the price movement among those top 30 names. So while many stocks participated, a few did the heavy lifting.

Is It Too Stretched To Keep Going?

The fund is certainly running warm. It now sits 11.3% above its 200-day moving average, a sign of its recent speed. Valuation is also a real consideration. The basket trades at about 22.5 times earnings, a step up from its roughly 5-year median of 20.0. That is richer than its own recent history, and it is a fact worth noting for any holder.

So What Is The Right Move Here?

With a stretched price and a richer valuation, the temptation to sell is real. But for a fund like VTV, that is often a mistake. This is a portfolio of 331 positions, designed for long-term compounding. Selling a diversified compounder just because it is working is one of the classic ways investors can leave gains on the table. The fund's deepest past fall was 17.0%, and its annualized price volatility is about 10%, a reminder that swings are part of the journey. But its five-year total return of +81% shows what patience can deliver. The most sensible action is often to do nothing and let the compounding continue. Of course, if this run-up has made VTV a much larger part of your portfolio than you planned, trimming it back to your target allocation is always a prudent move. The question of when to take gains on a value fund is a common one for investors.

Ultimately, a new high is not a sell signal. It is the result of a process working as intended. Unless your long-term plan has changed, the data here suggests letting that process keep working for you.

Is There A Stronger ETF To Own Instead?

Whether you are inclined to keep holding or tempted to take the gain and look elsewhere, the same question follows: is there simply a better ETF to own right now? A new high tells you the price is up, not whether VTV still stacks up against its peers on valuation, return, and risk.

How Much Is Riding On A Few Names?

The single largest holding, SK Hynix, represents 23% of the entire fund. This heavy weighting means that while you own dozens of companies, the fund behaves like about 10 equally weighted holdings.

The portfolio's tilt is just as pronounced at the industry level. Information Technology is the largest sector at 48% of the fund. Within that broad category, the weight is further focused. A fund's name gives you the geography, but its composition gives you the actual bet. For EWY, that bet is heavily tilted toward a handful of technology-related companies. Even the steadiest funds can give back gains; in the past, the iShares Select Dividend ETF (DVY) has seen its price fall as much as 17.5% from a prior peak. This is a fund designed to track an index of established, dividend-paying U.S. companies, a basket of names like Altria and Prudential Financial. And right now, it is anything but down. The fund just closed at $162.99, a new record high after a +6.3% run over the past three months. A new high always brings a question to the surface: what, if anything, should you do now?

How Broad Was The Climb?

The first thing to check is the quality of the advance. Was this a real rally or was it just a few hot stocks pulling the whole fund higher? The evidence points to a broad and healthy move. The fund's largest holdings span 8 sectors, so you are not overly exposed to one corner of the market, though Financials do represent about 33% of those top names. More importantly, over the past three months, 28 of the 30 largest holdings rose. The three biggest movers accounted for only about a quarter of the price movement among that group. This was not a narrow sprint; it was a widely shared advance.

Is The Price Getting Stretched?

A broad move is good, but it does not mean a fund cannot be expensive. DVY now sits about 9.6% above its 200-day moving average, showing how quickly it has run. On valuation, the basket trades at about 16.6 times earnings. That is richer than its own history; the fund's roughly 5-year median is 13.7. So yes, you are holding this basket at a higher multiple than is typical for it. With an annualized price volatility of about 11%, you should always be prepared for swings, but the current price is clearly elevated relative to its recent trend and historical valuation.

So, What Is The Right Move?

When a diversified fund hits a new high on the back of a broad advance, the most sensible action is often the hardest: do nothing. This is what compounding looks like. The fund is doing its job, and selling a quality compounder simply because the price is up is a classic investor mistake. The richer valuation deserves attention, but for a long-term holder, trying to time an exit and re-entry can easily do more harm than good. This question of how to handle a dividend fund at a new peak is a common one. Your diversified ETF portfolio may be leaning heavily on a single railroad stock that has run far ahead of its trend.

Your fund portfolio feels diversified, but a single stock you never explicitly chose may have quietly become a major holding. Union Pacific (UNP), one of the largest railroad operators in North America, is now held across 48 different equity funds. After a powerful run-up, this one name could be carrying more weight in your returns and your risk than you realize.

How Stretched Has This One Stock Become?

Union Pacific has had a strong year, with the stock returning +36%. It now trades at $307.32, which is about 24% above its 200-day moving average, a common measure of its medium-term trend. Investors have priced in high expectations, with the stock trading at about 24 times its expected earnings for the year ahead, while profits are forecast to grow about 10% a year.

Which Of Your Funds Are Along For The Ride?

This performance has been a boon for the funds most concentrated in the stock. The iShares U.S. Transportation ETF (IYT), for example, holds UNP at about 17.1% of the fund. That heavy concentration helped power its +24% return over the past year. Other funds carry it at lower, but still meaningful, weights. The State Street Industrial Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLI) holds UNP at about 3.2% of its assets and returned +20% over the past year. The exposure is widespread, but the concentration varies significantly from one fund to the next.

What A Simple Pullback Would Cost

This is not a prediction, but a simple scenario to make the risk concrete. If UNP simply fell back to its 200-day average, the stock would drop about 20% from its current price. For the funds holding it, the impact is direct. In that scenario, the iShares U.S. Transportation ETF (IYT) would lose about 3.3% of its value from this one holding alone. For the State Street Industrial Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLI), the same move would cause a loss of about 0.6%.

This exposure is also sticky. You can't surgically sell just the UNP shares inside your ETF. To reduce your position, you would have to sell the entire fund, which could trigger a taxable capital gain, making it difficult to trim the very position that has grown the largest.

An Option To Keep The Theme, Not The Concentration

For investors who want to maintain exposure to the industrial sector with less single-stock risk, there are alternatives. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Industrials ETF (RSPN) holds UNP at about 1.3% of the fund. That is a fraction of the 17.1% weight in the iShares U.S. Transportation ETF (IYT). The performance reflects this difference in strategy: over the past year, RSPN returned +14%, versus +24% for IYT. The lower concentration meant it didn't capture as much of UNP's sharp run, but it also carries far less risk from this single name.

The popular tech-heavy fund isn't expensive by its own standards, but the real question is what you're giving up to own it.

The basket of companies inside the Invesco QQQ Trust, Series 1 (QQQ) offers an aggregate earnings yield of 2.9%, while a 10-year US Treasury yields 4.7% today. That simple comparison is the starting point for any serious look at this fund. After a run that has seen it return +22% over the trailing twelve months, the central question for a potential buyer is straightforward: is the price you pay for this fund justified by what is actually inside it?

A Price Tag That Looks Familiar

By one important measure, the fund's price tag is quite ordinary. The fund's trailing price-to-earnings ratio, a classic valuation yardstick, is 34.1. That figure sits just a hair above its 5-year average of 33.6. This tells you that, relative to its own recent history, the fund isn't trading at a notable premium or a discount. You are paying a price that investors have, on average, deemed fair for this basket over the past several years.

The fund's consensus forward price-to-earnings ratio is about 21.4. It's tempting to see the drop from the trailing 34.1 as a sign of significant growth ahead, but be careful. The forward multiple is a non-GAAP figure computed across only the fund's profitable holdings, so it is NOT directly comparable to the trailing P/E, which is GAAP and includes all holdings. The gap between them is a statistical artifact, not a pure market expectation of earnings growth.

The Engine Powering The Price

So, what does that fair-looking price get you? Growth, and plenty of it. Across the fund's largest holdings, trailing twelve-month earnings per share grew about 64% over the past year. Looking ahead, consensus estimates put one-year earnings growth for the fund's holdings at about 23%. This is the core of the argument for owning the fund. The valuation is supported by the powerful earnings expansion of the companies it holds.

The Yield You're Giving Up

Here is the trade-off. That earnings yield of 2.9% sits about 1.8 percentage points below the 4.7% risk-free Treasury yield. This is what's known as a negative risk premium. In plain terms, you are not being compensated with a higher yield for taking on the risks of owning stocks compared to holding a government bond. Instead, you are paying for access to that growth, with the expectation that future appreciation will more than make up for the income you are forgoing today.

This is a fund driven by a few key players. Its five largest holdings make up 30% of the fund, led by names like Nvidia (NVDA) at 8.1% and Apple (AAPL) at 7.9%. The performance of the NASDAQ-100 Index it tracks, and therefore your return, is heavily influenced by the fortunes of a small handful of very large companies. When you buy the index, you are buying their story. The decision to own the fund today comes down to whether you believe that powerful growth is worth paying for, even when a safer alternative offers a higher immediate yield. The thing to watch is whether that estimated 23% earnings growth materializes; the current price is counting on it.
